reasons: The tool is small, has three subcommands, and one person will maintain it for years. argparse subparsers cover this with no third-party dependency to track.
argparse ships with Python and follows its release cycle. It has no dependency pins, no advisories to watch, and no risk of an upstream API break over a multi-year life.

click and typer are both healthy, but they add a dependency to install and update. typer also pulls in click, and in recent versions rich and other packages. That is more surface than three subcommands need.
Strongest point against A: it has more boilerplate, and typer's type-hint style is more pleasant to write. That is a small one-time cost at this size. It does not outweigh years of dependency upkeep.

Nothing in argparse is being phased out. Recent CPython releases have added features to it, such as colored help and better error suggestions in 3.14. Python 3.11 is the pinned version and does not have these.
risks: I did no web search this session, so I cannot cite dated releases. From memory, argparse gained colored help and suggest_on_error in Python 3.14 (Oct 2025), and typer and click are both actively released. I did not check any of this against a source.
If the tool later grows to many nested subcommands, shell completion, or heavy validation, argparse becomes verbose and a move to click would be warranted.
The brief does not say whether the repo already uses click or typer elsewhere. If it does, consistency would favor that library.
would_change_if: The repo already depends on click or typer, or the tool is expected to grow well beyond three simple subcommands. In either case I would pick B.
